osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.md:
(Childhood osteoarticular infection is covered in detail in the Paediatric Ortho note "bone and joint infection in children"; spondylodiscitis in the Spine notes; prosthetic joint infection in the Arthroplasty notes. This note concentrates on adults and general principles.)

## 1. Definitions and classification
- **Osteomyelitis:** infection of bone and marrow with progressive inflammatory destruction and new bone formation.
- **Waldvogel classification (by pathogenesis and duration):**
  - **Haematogenous** (children: long-bone metaphysis; adults: **vertebrae commonest**).
  - **Contiguous focus** (open fracture, surgery, implant, adjacent soft-tissue infection), **with or without vascular insufficiency** (diabetic foot, peripheral vascular disease).
  - **Acute vs chronic:** chronic is defined by **dead bone (sequestrum)**, not strictly by time (traditionally over about 6 weeks of symptoms).
- **Pathological hallmarks of chronic osteomyelitis:** **sequestrum** (dead bone, avascular, harbours biofilm), **involucrum** (reactive periosteal new bone), **cloaca** (hole in the involucrum), **sinus tract** to skin.

### Cierny-Mader staging (adult osteomyelitis; most-examined)
**Anatomical type**

| Type | Description | Treatment implication |
|---|---|---|
| **I Medullary** | Endosteal/intramedullary infection (haematogenous, **infected intramedullary nail**) | **Unroofing/reaming of the canal**, implant removal, antibiotics |
| **II Superficial** | Infection of the outer cortical surface secondary to a **soft-tissue coverage defect** | **Superficial decortication plus soft-tissue cover** (flap) |
| **III Localised** | Full-thickness cortical sequestration that can be excised **without loss of stability** | **Debridement, dead-space management**; bone remains stable |
| **IV Diffuse** | Through-and-through, **mechanically unstable** before or after debridement (e.g. **infected nonunion**) | **Debridement plus stabilisation plus bone reconstruction** |

**Physiological host**

| Host | Description |
|---|---|
| **A** | Normal host: normal physiology, immune and vascular status |
| **B** | Compromised: **Bs systemic** (diabetes, malnutrition, renal or hepatic failure, immunosuppression, malignancy, extremes of age, chronic hypoxia, smoking), **Bl local** (chronic lymphoedema, venous stasis, major vessel disease, arteritis, extensive scarring, radiation fibrosis, neuropathy), **Bls** both |
| **C** | **Treatment worse than the disease** (morbidity of surgery exceeds that of the infection): suppressive antibiotics or palliation, or amputation |

- **Clinical stage = anatomical type + host** (e.g. **stage IV Bs**). Correcting B-host factors (glycaemic control, smoking cessation, nutrition, revascularisation) converts to a better host.

## 2. Microbiology and pathogenesis
- **Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism** in all forms (haematogenous, post-traumatic, septic arthritis). **MRSA** is increasing.
- **Coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis)** and **Cutibacterium acnes (shoulder)**: implant-associated infection.
- **Biofilm:** bacteria adhere to dead bone or implants (S. aureus via **MSCRAMM adhesins**), secrete an extracellular polysaccharide matrix (**glycocalyx**), become metabolically dormant and up to **1000 times more resistant to antibiotics**; host defences cannot penetrate. Hence **dead bone and loose implants must be removed**. **Small-colony variants** and intracellular persistence explain relapse.
- **Rifampicin** is active against biofilm staphylococci (always in combination, never monotherapy because resistance develops rapidly); **fluoroquinolones** for Gram-negative biofilm.

### Organisms by setting
| Setting | Characteristic organism |
|---|---|
| **All ages, most infections** | **S. aureus** |
| **Sickle cell disease** | **Salmonella** (S. aureus still common) |
| **IV drug users** | **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**, S. aureus (MRSA), Candida; unusual sites: **sternoclavicular, sacroiliac, pubic symphysis, spine** |
| **Puncture wound through a shoe** | **Pseudomonas** |
| **Diabetic foot** | **Polymicrobial** (S. aureus, streptococci, Gram-negatives, anaerobes) |
| **Prosthesis or implant** | Coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus; **C. acnes** in shoulder |
| **Human bite (fight bite)** | **Eikenella corrodens** plus streptococci and anaerobes |
| **Cat or dog bite** | **Pasteurella multocida** (cat bites especially) |
| **Fish tank, marine injury** | **Mycobacterium marinum** (granulomatous tenosynovitis of the hand; culture at 30-32 C) |
| **Rose thorn, gardener** | **Sporothrix schenckii** (lymphocutaneous) |
| **Seawater, raw shellfish, liver disease** | Vibrio vulnificus (necrotising) |
| **Farm, unpasteurised milk (India, Middle East)** | **Brucella** (sacroiliitis, spondylitis) |
| **Sexually active young adult** | **Neisseria gonorrhoeae** (septic arthritis) |
| **Haemodialysis, chronic lines** | S. aureus, Gram-negatives |
| **Chronic granulomatous disease** | Aspergillus, catalase-positive organisms (Serratia) |
| **India, insidious mono-arthritis or dactylitis** | **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** (see tuberculosis note) |

## 3. Clinical presentation (adults)
- **Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in adults** is uncommon outside the spine; consider immunosuppression, IV drug use, sickle cell disease, dialysis, endocarditis.
- **Post-traumatic and post-operative infection:** wound erythema, persistent drainage, **sinus**, implant failure, nonunion; pain may be minimal.
- **Chronic osteomyelitis:** recurrent flares with discharging sinus, sequestrum extrusion, systemic signs often absent.
  - **Marjolin ulcer:** **squamous cell carcinoma** in a long-standing sinus (latency usually **decades**); suspect with increased pain, foul or bloody discharge, everted edges, a fungating mass. **Biopsy**; usually treated by **amputation** or wide excision.
  - **Amyloidosis** (secondary AA) in long-standing chronic infection.
- **Diabetic foot osteomyelitis:** a positive **probe-to-bone test** (high positive predictive value in high-risk patients), ulcer over 2 cm2 or deeper than 3 mm, ESR over 70 mm/h. Distinguish from **Charcot neuroarthropathy** (midfoot, no ulcer, MRI marrow oedema periarticular and subchondral vs infection at ulcer sites).

## 4. Investigations
### Blood tests
- **WBC** (often normal in chronic infection), **ESR** and **CRP** (CRP the best to follow response), **blood cultures** (positive mainly in haematogenous and acute disease).

### Imaging
| Test | Use and key points |
|---|---|
| **Plain radiographs** | First test; **bone changes lag about 10-21 days** (need 30-50% loss of mineral): periosteal reaction, lysis, sequestrum (dense, sharply marginated), involucrum, implant loosening |
| **MRI** | **Investigation of choice for acute osteomyelitis** and spinal infection: marrow oedema (**low T1, high T2/STIR**), abscess (rim enhancement), sinus tracts. **Normal MRI essentially excludes osteomyelitis.** Limited by metal artefact |
| **"Penumbra sign" (MRI T1)** | A rim of **slightly higher T1 signal (granulation tissue) lining an abscess cavity**: characteristic of **subacute osteomyelitis/Brodie abscess** (helps distinguish from tumour) |
| **CT** | Best to show **sequestra**, cortical destruction, sinus and cloaca; plan debridement |
| **Three-phase Tc-99m bone scan** | Highly sensitive (positive in all three phases), **poor specificity** after trauma, surgery, Charcot or tumour |
| **Labelled leucocyte (In-111 or Tc-99m HMPAO) scan** | Better specificity for infection with **recent fracture or implants**; less useful in the **axial skeleton** (infection may appear cold); combine with **marrow (sulphur colloid) scan** to improve accuracy |
| **FDG PET-CT** | High accuracy for **chronic osteomyelitis** and the **axial skeleton**; less affected by metal; cannot reliably separate infection from early post-operative healing |
| **Sinogram** | Rarely used now; shows sinus tract communication |

### Microbiology and histology (the gold standard)
- **Bone biopsy (open or image-guided) for culture and histology is the definitive diagnostic test**.
- **Stop antibiotics about 2 weeks before sampling** in the stable patient (not in sepsis).
- **Take at least 3, ideally 5 or more, separate deep tissue samples with clean instruments**; **2 or more samples growing the same organism** confirms infection (one positive may be a contaminant, especially for low-virulence skin organisms).
- **Sinus tract swabs are unreliable** (colonising flora), except that **S. aureus from a sinus correlates reasonably with deep culture**.
- **Sonication** of removed implants increases culture yield; **16S rRNA PCR** for culture-negative cases; **extended culture (10-14 days)** for C. acnes and fastidious organisms.
- **Histology:** acute (neutrophils, necrosis), chronic (lymphocytes, plasma cells, fibrosis, necrotic bone), granulomas (TB, fungal); also excludes malignancy.

## 5. Treatment principles
### Acute osteomyelitis
- **Antibiotics** guided by culture; empirical anti-staphylococcal cover (add vancomycin where MRSA is prevalent).
- **Surgery** for abscess drainage, necrotic bone, failure to respond within 48-72 hours, or infected implants.
- **Duration:** traditionally **about 6 weeks** for adult osteomyelitis; **vertebral osteomyelitis 6 weeks is as effective as 12 weeks** (**Bernard et al., Lancet 2015**).

### Oral vs IV antibiotics: OVIVA trial
- **Li et al., NEJM 2019 (OVIVA):** in adults with bone and joint infection (including implant-related), **oral antibiotics were non-inferior to IV** during the first 6 weeks (treatment failure about 13% oral vs 15% IV), with fewer line complications and shorter stay.
- **Agents with good oral bioavailability and bone penetration:** **fluoroquinolones**, **rifampicin (in combination)**, **linezolid**, **clindamycin**, **co-trimoxazole**, **doxycycline**, high-dose beta-lactams (e.g. flucloxacillin, amoxicillin).
- **MRSA options:** vancomycin, teicoplanin, **daptomycin**, **linezolid** (myelosuppression and neuropathy with long courses), co-trimoxazole, doxycycline, clindamycin (if susceptible).

### Chronic osteomyelitis: surgical principles
1. **Optimise the host** (diabetes, smoking, nutrition, vascular status); decide treatment intent (curative vs suppressive vs amputation).
2. **Radical debridement:** excise all **sinus tracts, scar, sequestra and devitalised bone**, back to **healthy bleeding bone ("paprika sign")**, like a tumour resection. Inadequate debridement is the commonest cause of failure. **Wait for a mature involucrum** before sequestrectomy in children and when the involucrum must carry load.
3. **Deep samples** (5 or more) for culture and histology.
4. **Dead-space management:**
   - **Antibiotic-loaded PMMA beads or spacer** (Buchholz principle): high local antibiotic levels; non-absorbable, so removal or exchange is needed. **Heat-stable antibiotics only: gentamicin, tobramycin, vancomycin** (also clindamycin, cefazolin); **high dose (several grams per 40 g packet) for treatment, low dose (about 1 g per 40 g) for prophylaxis**. Elution is greatest in the first days.
   - **Absorbable carriers:** **calcium sulphate** (wound drainage, transient hypercalcaemia), calcium sulphate/hydroxyapatite composites, antibiotic-loaded bioactive glass.
   - **Muscle flap** filling (local or free).
5. **Bone reconstruction (segmental defects):**
   - **Masquelet induced-membrane technique:** stage 1 debridement, stabilisation and a **PMMA cement spacer**, which induces a vascular **membrane secreting growth factors (VEGF, TGF-beta, BMP-2)**; stage 2 at about **4-8 weeks** the spacer is removed, the membrane preserved and the cavity packed with **cancellous autograft** (iliac crest or **RIA, reamer-irrigator-aspirator**).
   - **Ilizarov bone transport (distraction osteogenesis):** corticotomy, **latency about 5-7 days**, **distraction about 1 mm/day in 4 increments of 0.25 mm**, consolidation (healing index roughly 1-1.5 months per cm in adults); docking-site problems are common.
   - **Vascularised fibular graft**; **Papineau open cancellous grafting** (historical); acute shortening with later lengthening.
6. **Stabilisation:** **external fixation (monolateral or circular)** in the infected field, or antibiotic-coated nails; exchange to definitive fixation once infection is controlled.
7. **Soft-tissue cover (tibia):** **proximal third: gastrocnemius (medial head) flap**; **middle third: soleus flap**; **distal third: free flap** (or fasciocutaneous/reverse sural flap).
8. **Antibiotics after debridement:** usually **about 6 weeks** (OVIVA supports early oral switch).
9. **Amputation** for C-hosts, failed reconstruction, Marjolin ulcer, or patient preference after repeated failure.

## 6. Fracture-related infection (FRI)
### Consensus definition (Metsemakers et al., Injury 2018; updated by Govaert et al., JBJS 2020)
- **Confirmatory criteria (any one confirms FRI):**
  - **Fistula, sinus or wound breakdown** communicating with the bone or implant.
  - **Purulent drainage** from the wound or **pus** at surgery.
  - **Phenotypically indistinguishable pathogens in at least 2 separate deep tissue or implant (including sonication fluid) specimens**.
  - **Histopathology:** microorganisms in deep tissue, or (2020 update) **more than 5 neutrophils per high-power field** in chronic or late-onset cases.
- **Suggestive criteria (prompt further work-up):** clinical signs (pain, redness, swelling, warmth, fever), radiological signs (lysis, loosening, sequestrum, failure of healing, periosteal reaction), a pathogen in a single deep sample, raised serum markers, **new or persistent wound drainage beyond the first few days**.

### Timing and treatment (Willenegger and Roth timing)
| Onset after fixation | Typical approach |
|---|---|
| **Early (under 2 weeks)** | **Debridement, irrigation, implant retention (if stable)**, antibiotics; biofilm immature |
| **Delayed (2-10 weeks)** | Debridement; retain if implant stable and fracture healing progressing, otherwise exchange |
| **Late (over 10 weeks)** | Mature biofilm: **implant removal or exchange**, debridement, stabilisation, often staged reconstruction |

- **Key principle:** **fracture stability is essential for both bone healing and infection control**; a stable implant may be retained until union, then removed. Loose implants must be removed.
- **Antibiotic duration (FRI consensus):** **about 12 weeks when the implant is retained**, **about 6 weeks when it is removed or exchanged**; **rifampicin** combination for staphylococci with retained implants, fluoroquinolones for Gram-negatives.
- **Prevention in open fractures:** early antibiotics (within 1 hour), thorough debridement, early soft-tissue cover (within 72 hours to 7 days per BOAST), local antibiotics (see Trauma notes).

## 7. Septic arthritis in adults
### Epidemiology and risk factors
- **Knee is commonest (about 50%)**, then hip, shoulder, ankle, wrist. Polyarticular in 10-20% (**rheumatoid arthritis**, sepsis, gonococcal): higher mortality.
- **Risk factors:** **rheumatoid arthritis (strongest)**, **age over 80**, **diabetes**, **prosthetic joint**, recent joint surgery or **intra-articular injection**, skin infection or ulcers, IV drug use, immunosuppression, alcoholism, haemodialysis.
- **Organisms:** **S. aureus commonest**; streptococci second; **Gram-negatives** in the elderly, IV drug users and immunocompromised; **N. gonorrhoeae** in sexually active young adults (the commonest cause of septic arthritis in this group in some series).
- **Cartilage destruction** begins within hours (bacterial toxins, **neutrophil proteases and MMPs**, cytokines IL-1 and TNF-alpha); **mortality about 10%** (higher with polyarticular disease and RA).

### Diagnosis
- Hot, swollen, painful joint with **painful restriction of all movements**; fever in only about half.
- **Joint aspiration before antibiotics is mandatory** (aseptic technique; avoid cellulitic skin): **Gram stain** (positive in about 50%), **culture** (positive in about 80% of non-gonococcal infections; inoculate blood-culture bottles), **cell count**, **crystals**.
- **Blood cultures** (positive in about a third to a half).
- **Crystals do not exclude infection** (gout or CPPD can coexist with sepsis).

| Synovial fluid | WBC per mm3 | Neutrophils | Other |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Normal** | Under 200 | Under 25% | Clear, viscous |
| **Non-inflammatory (OA, trauma)** | 200-2,000 | Under 25% | Clear yellow |
| **Inflammatory (RA, gout, CPPD, reactive)** | 2,000-50,000 (can be higher) | Over 50% | Cloudy; crystals in gout/CPPD |
| **Septic** | **Over 50,000 (often over 100,000)** | **Over 75-90%** | Turbid or purulent, **low glucose (under 50% of serum)**, high lactate |

- **Crystal identification under polarised light:** **gout: needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent monosodium urate (yellow when parallel)**; **CPPD: rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent**.
- **Prosthetic joint infection uses much lower thresholds** (e.g. chronic PJI synovial WBC over about 3,000 cells and over about 80% neutrophils per ICM 2018; see Arthroplasty notes).

### Treatment
- **Urgent joint drainage plus antibiotics** (an orthopaedic emergency).
- **Drainage options:** **arthroscopic lavage** (preferred for the knee, shoulder, ankle; allows debridement and synovectomy), **open arthrotomy** (**hip**, failed arthroscopy, advanced stages, inaccessible joints), **repeated needle aspiration** (selected patients unfit for surgery; evidence shows comparable outcomes in some joints, debated).
- **Gachter arthroscopic staging of septic arthritis (guides surgery):**

| Stage | Arthroscopic findings | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | Cloudy fluid, synovial redness, possible petechial bleeding | Arthroscopic lavage |
| **II** | Severe synovitis, **fibrin deposition, pus** | Arthroscopic lavage and debridement |
| **III** | **Thickened synovium, compartment formation ("sponge-like")** | Arthroscopic synovectomy (repeat procedures may be needed) |
| **IV** | **Aggressive pannus infiltrating and undermining cartilage**, radiological **subchondral osteolysis** | **Open arthrotomy, synovectomy**, debridement |

- **Empirical antibiotics** after samples: anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam (cefazolin or flucloxacillin), **add vancomycin if MRSA risk**, add Gram-negative cover (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) in the elderly, immunocompromised or IV drug users.
- **Duration:** traditionally 4-6 weeks; **Gjika et al. (Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 2019): 2 weeks after surgical drainage was non-inferior to 4 weeks** for native-joint septic arthritis in adults. Typical current practice: **2-4 weeks with early oral switch** (longer with osteomyelitis or slow response).
- **Rehabilitation:** short splintage for pain, then **early active movement** (continuous passive motion improves cartilage nutrition, Salter).

### Gonococcal arthritis
- **Disseminated gonococcal infection triad: tenosynovitis, dermatitis (painless pustules), migratory polyarthralgia**, or a purulent mono-arthritis (knee, wrist, ankle).
- **Synovial culture positive in under 50%**; take **NAAT/cultures from urethra, cervix, rectum and pharynx** and blood cultures.
- **Treatment:** **ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily**, oral switch after improvement, **total about 7 days**; treat chlamydia co-infection (**doxycycline**) and partners. Surgical drainage rarely needed.

### Complications
- **Cartilage loss and secondary OA**, **fibrous or bony ankylosis**, **AVN of the femoral head** (hip), adjacent **osteomyelitis**, sepsis and death. Delay in drainage is the main predictor of poor outcome.

## 8. Special forms and differentials
- **Brodie abscess (subacute osteomyelitis):** well-defined metaphyseal lucency with a sclerotic rim, **penumbra sign** on MRI; differentials **osteoid osteoma** (nidus, night pain relieved by NSAIDs), chondroblastoma, LCH, Ewing. Curettage and antibiotics.
- **Sclerosing osteomyelitis of Garre:** low-grade infection with dense cortical thickening without abscess (jaw, long bones); differentials osteoid osteoma, Ewing, stress fracture.
- **Chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis (CRMO) and SAPHO syndrome** (Synovitis, Acne, Pustulosis, Hyperostosis, Osteitis): sterile, **anterior chest wall/sternoclavicular** in adults; NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, biologics.
- **Brucellosis:** **sacroiliitis** (young adults) and **spondylitis** (older adults, lumbar): **Pedro Pons sign** (anterosuperior endplate erosion), preserved vertebral architecture, little abscess; **doxycycline plus rifampicin (or streptomycin/gentamicin)** for at least 6 weeks (spondylitis about 12 weeks).
- **Necrotising fasciitis:** pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus, systemic toxicity; **LRINEC score** supports but does not exclude; **emergency radical debridement** plus broad-spectrum antibiotics including **clindamycin** (toxin suppression). Type I polymicrobial, **type II group A streptococcus** (with or without S. aureus).
- **Pyomyositis (tropical):** S. aureus abscess within muscle (quadriceps, gluteal, psoas); ultrasound or MRI; drainage.
- **Differentials of an acute hot joint:** **gout and pseudogout** (commonest mimic), reactive arthritis, RA flare, haemarthrosis (haemophilia, anticoagulants, PVNS), Lyme disease, cellulitis or prepatellar bursitis (painless joint motion in bursitis).

> Exam pearl: **S. aureus is the commonest organism everywhere; Salmonella in sickle cell; Pseudomonas in IV drug users and sneaker puncture; Eikenella in human bites; Pasteurella in cat bites; M. marinum in fish tanks.** **Cierny-Mader: I medullary, II superficial, III localised (stable), IV diffuse (unstable); host A, B (s/l), C.**

> Exam pearl: **MRI is the investigation of choice for acute osteomyelitis; CT best for sequestra; FDG PET-CT for chronic and axial infection.** **Bone biopsy with 5 deep samples (2 matching = infection) is the gold standard; sinus swabs are unreliable.** **OVIVA: oral equals IV in the first 6 weeks.** **Debride to paprika-sign bleeding bone.**

> Exam pearl: **Septic arthritis: knee commonest, RA the strongest risk factor, synovial WBC over 50,000 with over 90% neutrophils, crystals do not exclude infection.** **Gachter stages I-III arthroscopic, IV open.** **Gonococcal: tenosynovitis + pustules + migratory polyarthralgia, ceftriaxone.**

tuberculosis.md:
(Spinal tuberculosis, Pott's paraplegia and its surgery are covered in detail in the Spine note "spinal tuberculosis and infection"; childhood dactylitis is also mentioned in Paediatric Ortho. This note covers general principles and extraspinal osteoarticular TB.)

## 1. Epidemiology and pathogenesis
- **India has the largest TB burden in the world.** **Osteoarticular TB forms about 1-3% of all TB** and about 10-15% of extrapulmonary TB.
- **Order of frequency:** **spine (about 50%)**, then **hip**, then **knee**; then foot and ankle, elbow, wrist and hand, shoulder, sacroiliac joint.
- **Organism:** **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** (acid-fast, aerobic, slow-growing, doubling time about 15-20 hours); M. bovis rarely (unpasteurised milk).
- **Always secondary:** **haematogenous spread from a primary focus** (lung, lymph nodes, kidney), which may be quiescent; **active pulmonary disease is present in under half** of patients with osteoarticular TB.
- **Pathology:** **epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells and central caseous necrosis**; a cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction.
  - **Cold abscess:** caseous material and debris without signs of acute inflammation, tracks along fascial planes and neurovascular bundles, may burst to form a **sinus** (secondary pyogenic infection then common).
  - **Paucibacillary disease:** few organisms in bone and joint lesions, so smears are often negative.
- **Joint involvement starts as synovial or osseous disease:**
  - **Synovial:** granulation tissue (pannus) spreads over the cartilage margins and erodes the **bare areas (peripheral, non-weight-bearing) first**: **marginal erosions**.
  - **Osseous:** metaphyseal or epiphyseal focus breaks into the joint.
  - **Cartilage is destroyed slowly** (proteolytic enzymes are less abundant than in pyogenic infection), so **joint space is preserved until late**.
- **Risk factors:** HIV (strongest), malnutrition, diabetes, alcohol, **immunosuppression and anti-TNF biologics** (screen before starting), chronic kidney disease, close contact, overcrowding, prior incompletely treated TB.

## 2. Clinical features (general)
- **Insidious onset**, chronic **monoarticular** pain and swelling, often weeks to months; **constitutional symptoms** (evening rise of temperature, night sweats, anorexia, weight loss) in only some patients.
- **Night cries** in children (protective muscle spasm relaxes in sleep, painful movement wakes the child).
- **Marked muscle wasting** out of proportion to the joint findings; **boggy synovial thickening**; warmth without redness.
- **Restricted, painful movements in all directions**; deformity due to spasm, then destruction.
- **Cold abscess and sinuses**, regional lymphadenopathy.
- **Healed disease ends in fibrous ankylosis** (painful, some motion); **bony ankylosis** is more typical of pyogenic infection (secondary infection of a TB joint can lead to bony ankylosis).

## 3. Investigations
### Laboratory
- **ESR raised** (non-specific; used to follow disease activity), CRP, relative **lymphocytosis**, anaemia.
- **Mantoux test** (tuberculin skin test; **10 mm or more induration at 48-72 hours** positive; 5 mm in HIV) and **IGRA** (QuantiFERON, not affected by BCG): indicate infection, not active disease; **of limited value in endemic India**; negative tests do not exclude TB (immunosuppression, miliary disease).
- **Chest radiograph** (healed or active pulmonary lesion), HIV testing, glucose, liver and renal function before ATT.

### Synovial fluid
- Turbid, **WBC typically about 10,000-20,000 per mm3** (variable), **lymphocytes predominate** (neutrophils can predominate early), **high protein, low glucose**, poor mucin clot.
- Smear for AFB usually negative (positive in a minority); culture positive in a larger proportion but slow.

### Tissue diagnosis (biopsy is the gold standard)
- **Synovial biopsy** (arthroscopic or open) or image-guided bone biopsy: **histology** (caseating granulomas) plus microbiology from the same tissue.
- **Ziehl-Neelsen smear for AFB:** low sensitivity (paucibacillary).
- **Culture:** **liquid culture (MGIT) about 1-3 weeks**, **solid Lowenstein-Jensen medium about 4-8 weeks**; needed for full **drug susceptibility testing (DST)**.
- **CBNAAT/GeneXpert MTB/RIF (and Xpert Ultra):** rapid (about 2 hours) nucleic acid amplification test that detects **M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance**; **recommended initial diagnostic test by WHO and India's NTEP** for extrapulmonary samples. A negative result does not exclude TB.
- **Line probe assay (LPA):** detects isoniazid and rifampicin resistance (first-line LPA) and fluoroquinolone/injectable resistance (second-line LPA).
- **Rifampicin resistance is used as a surrogate for MDR-TB.**

### Imaging
- **Radiographs:** changes appear late. **Phemister triad of tuberculous arthritis:**
  1. **Juxta-articular osteoporosis** (osteopenia, the earliest sign).
  2. **Peripheral (marginal) erosions** of bone.
  3. **Gradual narrowing of the joint space** (late, because cartilage is relatively preserved).
- **"Kissing" lesions or sequestra:** erosions or wedge-shaped sequestra on opposite sides of a joint (knee, sacroiliac).
- **MRI:** **investigation of choice for early diagnosis** and extent: synovial thickening (low T2 signal of hypertrophied synovium in some), marrow oedema, erosions, cold abscesses with **thin smooth enhancing rims**, rice bodies, and skip lesions in the spine.
- **Ultrasound:** effusion, synovial thickening, abscess, guided aspiration.
- **CT:** bony destruction, sequestra, guided biopsy.

### Differential diagnosis of chronic monoarthritis (common distractors)
| Condition | Distinguishing features |
|---|---|
| **Rheumatoid (monoarticular onset)** | Symmetrical later, RF/anti-CCP positive, no caseation |
| **Pyogenic (low-grade, partially treated)** | Rapid joint space loss, sclerosis, bony ankylosis, neutrophilic fluid |
| **Pigmented villonodular synovitis (TGCT)** | Knee in young adults, **haemorrhagic fluid**, **haemosiderin "blooming" on MRI gradient echo**, preserved joint space |
| **Haemophilic arthropathy** | Male, recurrent haemarthroses, widened intercondylar notch, squared patella |
| **Fungal and brucellar arthritis** | Exposure history, culture, serology |
| **Juvenile idiopathic arthritis** | Children, uveitis, growth disturbance |
| **Perthes, transient synovitis (children's hip)** | Normal ESR, typical imaging |

## 4. Antitubercular therapy (ATT)
### First-line drugs
| Drug | Daily dose (mg/kg) | Action | Key toxicity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Isoniazid (H)** | 5 (4-6) | Bactericidal (rapidly multiplying) | **Hepatitis**, **peripheral neuropathy** (give **pyridoxine**), lupus-like syndrome |
| **Rifampicin (R)** | 10 (8-12) | Bactericidal, **sterilising** (semi-dormant bacilli) | **Hepatitis**, **orange-red body fluids**, flu-like syndrome, thrombocytopenia, **enzyme induction** (oral contraceptives, warfarin, antiretrovirals) |
| **Pyrazinamide (Z)** | 25 (20-30) | Sterilising (intracellular, acid pH) | **Hepatitis (most hepatotoxic)**, **hyperuricaemia/gout**, arthralgia |
| **Ethambutol (E)** | 15 (15-20) | Bacteriostatic; prevents resistance | **Optic (retrobulbar) neuritis: loss of red-green colour vision**, reduced acuity |
| Streptomycin (S) | 15 | Bactericidal (injectable) | **Ototoxicity (vestibular), nephrotoxicity** |

### Regimens and duration
- **India NTEP (daily fixed-dose combinations):** **intensive phase 2 months HRZE**, then **continuation phase HRE**. The standard total is 6 months for most TB, but **the continuation phase may be extended by 3-6 months for bone and joint TB** (and CNS TB), so **total 9-12 months** for osteoarticular TB is usual Indian orthopaedic practice.
- **International guidelines** (WHO, ATS/CDC/IDSA) accept **6-9 months for bone and joint TB** (many extend spinal TB to 9-12 months). Duration is **debated**; for exams the safe answer in India is **9-12 months, extended up to 18 months for slow responders**.
- **Monitoring:** clinical response (pain, weight, appetite), **ESR**, radiographs, **MRI healing signs**; liver function tests in those at risk.
- **Drug-induced hepatitis:** stop hepatotoxic drugs if transaminases exceed 5 times normal (or 3 times with symptoms) or bilirubin rises; reintroduce sequentially (rifampicin, then isoniazid; pyrazinamide often omitted) once liver function recovers.
- **Paradoxical reaction:** temporary worsening (enlarging abscess, new lesion) after starting ATT, especially in HIV (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, **IRIS**). It is not treatment failure; continue ATT but **exclude drug resistance** (repeat sampling).

### Drug-resistant TB
- **Mono/poly-resistant:** resistance to drugs other than both H and R.
- **MDR-TB:** resistance to **at least isoniazid and rifampicin**.
- **Pre-XDR TB:** MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to a **fluoroquinolone**.
- **XDR-TB (WHO 2021 definition):** MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to a **fluoroquinolone and at least one of bedaquiline or linezolid**.
- **Treatment:** **shorter all-oral regimens (e.g. 6-month BPaLM: bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin, per WHO 2022)** or longer individualised regimens (18-20 months); based on DST. Suspect resistance with poor response after about 3-5 months of compliant therapy.

### HIV co-infection
- Start ATT first; start **antiretroviral therapy within about 2 weeks** (later in TB meningitis); watch for IRIS and **rifampicin interactions** with protease inhibitors and some other antiretrovirals.

### Signs of healing
- **Clinical:** pain relief, weight gain, healed sinuses, normalised ESR.
- **Radiological:** **remineralisation**, **sharpening of articular and bony margins**, sclerosis, fusion or fibrous ankylosis.
- **MRI:** **fatty marrow replacement**, resolution of marrow oedema and abscess, reduced enhancement.

## 5. Role of surgery ("middle path" of Tuli)
- **ATT is the mainstay;** surgery supplements it. **Tuli's middle-path regimen:** ATT with rest, splintage and mobilisation; **surgery for specific indications** or failure to respond after about 3-6 months.
- **Indications for surgery:**
  - **Diagnostic biopsy** when the diagnosis is uncertain (and to obtain tissue for DST).
  - **Drainage of large cold abscesses** (aspiration through a **non-dependent, oblique, tangential track** through healthy skin to avoid a sinus) and excision of sinuses not responding.
  - **Synovectomy and joint debridement** (removal of pannus, sequestra, caseous material, loose cartilage) for synovial or early arthritic disease not responding to ATT.
  - **Sequestrectomy and curettage** of osseous foci near a joint (to prevent intra-articular spread).
  - **Correction of deformity and salvage** of the destroyed joint: arthrodesis, excision arthroplasty, osteotomy, **arthroplasty in healed disease**.
  - Spine: neurological deficit, instability, deformity (see Spine notes).
- **Arthroplasty in TB joints:** traditionally delayed until the disease had been **quiescent for about 10 years**; **current evidence supports total joint arthroplasty in healed disease and even in active disease when combined with thorough debridement and perioperative ATT** (commonly ATT started at least 2-6 weeks before and continued for 6-12 months after), with **low reactivation rates**. This is debated; the exam answer is "possible under ATT cover with radical debridement".

## 6. Tuberculosis of the hip
- **Second commonest site** (about 15% of osteoarticular TB); children and young adults.
- **Initial foci:** acetabular roof, femoral epiphysis, metaphysis (Babcock triangle region of the neck), greater trochanter, synovium.
- **Clinical and radiological stages (Tuli, Babhulkar and Pande):**

| Stage | Clinical attitude | Radiograph | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I Synovitis** | **Flexion, abduction, external rotation**; **apparent lengthening** (pelvic tilt) | Haziness of the articular margins, **osteopenia**, joint space preserved or increased | **ATT, traction, then mobilisation**: near-normal function expected |
| **II Early arthritis** | **Flexion, adduction, internal rotation**; **apparent shortening** | Marginal erosions, **reduced joint space** | ATT, traction, mobilisation; **synovectomy/debridement** if not responding |
| **III Advanced arthritis** | Flexion, adduction, internal rotation; **true shortening** | Marked destruction of head and acetabulum | ATT plus **joint debridement**; aim fibrous ankylosis in functional position, or later arthrodesis/arthroplasty |
| **IV Advanced arthritis with subluxation or dislocation** | Fixed deformity, gross true shortening | **Wandering (travelling) acetabulum**, pathological dislocation | **Girdlestone excision arthroplasty** or **arthrodesis**, or later **total hip arthroplasty** in healed disease |

- **Shanmugasundaram radiological types** of hip TB: **normal-looking**, **travelling (wandering) acetabulum**, **dislocating type**, **Perthes-like** (children), **protrusio acetabuli**, **atrophic**, and mortar-and-pestle types; they predict prognosis (Perthes-like and normal types have the best outcome).
- **Hip arthrodesis position:** about **20-30 degrees flexion, neutral to slight (0-5 degrees) adduction, slight external rotation (0-10 degrees)**; avoid abduction.
- **Differentials (children):** transient synovitis, Perthes disease, septic arthritis, JIA. **Adults:** AVN, inflammatory arthritis, PVNS, chondrolysis.

## 7. Tuberculosis of the knee
- **Third commonest site**; often synovial in origin; **marked synovial thickening ("boggy") and effusion**, quadriceps wasting.
- **Stages (Tuli):** **synovitis** (soft-tissue swelling, osteopenia), **early arthritis** (marginal erosions, joint space reduced), **advanced arthritis** (destruction, deformity), and **advanced arthritis with subluxation**.
- **Triple deformity of the knee** in advanced disease: **flexion, posterior subluxation and external rotation of the tibia** (also with valgus); due to hamstring and iliotibial band contracture.
- **Radiographs:** osteopenia, marginal erosions, **kissing sequestra** (femur and tibia); **widened intercondylar notch** is a distractor (haemophilia, JIA).
- **Treatment:** ATT, splint, mobilisation in early stages (good function expected); **arthroscopic or open synovectomy and debridement** if not responding; **arthrodesis (e.g. Charnley compression)** for painful destroyed joints in young labourers; **TKA in healed disease** (or under ATT cover).
- **Knee arthrodesis position:** about **0-15 degrees flexion, 5-8 degrees valgus, about 10 degrees external rotation**.

## 8. Other extraspinal sites
| Site | Key features |
|---|---|
| **Tuberculous dactylitis ("spina ventosa")** | Children (usually under about 6 years); **short tubular bones of the hand more than the foot** (proximal phalanx, metacarpals); **fusiform swelling and ballooned expanded bone with a thin cortex** ("spina ventosa" = bone inflated with air), periosteal reaction, sequestrum rare; heals with ATT, may cause shortening. **Differentials: syphilitic dactylitis (bilateral, symmetrical), sickle cell dactylitis (infants), enchondroma, pyogenic osteomyelitis, sarcoidosis** |
| **Shoulder** | Uncommon; adults; **"caries sicca"**: **dry, atrophic form with no pus or abscess**, marked wasting, painful stiffness, erosions of humeral head; differential frozen shoulder |
| **Elbow** | Relatively common upper-limb site; boggy swelling, early fixed flexion; olecranon or lateral condyle foci; good results with early ATT; excision arthroplasty or arthroplasty for destroyed joints |
| **Wrist and hand** | Wrist TB (destruction of carpals, "carpal crowding"); **compound palmar ganglion**: tuberculous tenosynovitis of the flexor sheaths (radial and ulnar bursae) with **cross-fluctuation above and below the flexor retinaculum** and **melon-seed (rice) bodies**; carpal tunnel syndrome; treated by ATT plus synovectomy |
| **Ankle and foot** | **Calcaneus** and talus commonest foot bones; sinuses common; may mimic chronic pyogenic osteomyelitis or a tumour |
| **Sacroiliac joint** | Young adults, unilateral, buttock or back pain, positive SI stress tests; erosions, widening then sclerosis; cold abscess in the buttock or iliac fossa; ATT, rarely debridement or fusion |
| **Greater trochanter and bursae** | Trochanteric TB (bursitis and erosion), cold abscess in the lateral thigh |
| **Long-bone shaft** | Rare; cystic or diaphyseal lesions mimic tumours (Ewing, LCH) |
| **Cystic TB of bone** | Children: multiple well-defined cystic lesions without sclerosis (differentials: LCH, sarcoid, fungal) |
| **Ribs, sternum, skull** | Cold abscesses, sinuses |
| **Poncet disease** | **Reactive (sterile) polyarthritis** in a patient with active TB elsewhere; resolves with ATT |

## 9. Atypical (non-tuberculous) mycobacteria and related
- **M. marinum:** fish tank or marine injury; **tenosynovitis or nodules of the hand**, sporotrichoid spread; culture at 30-32 C; clarithromycin with ethambutol or rifampicin, plus debridement.
- **M. avium complex, M. kansasii:** immunocompromised (HIV), tenosynovitis, osteomyelitis.
- **Rapidly growing mycobacteria (M. fortuitum, M. chelonae, M. abscessus):** **post-surgical and post-injection infections** (outbreaks after surgery or cosmetic procedures in India); resistant to standard ATT; macrolides, amikacin plus debridement.
- **BCG osteitis:** rare complication of BCG vaccination in infants (metaphyseal lesions); M. bovis BCG is **resistant to pyrazinamide**.

> Exam pearl: **Spine > hip > knee.** **Phemister triad: juxta-articular osteoporosis, peripheral erosions, gradual joint space narrowing** (pyogenic infection narrows the joint early). **Cold abscess, fibrous ankylosis, paucibacillary disease.** **Biopsy (histology plus CBNAAT plus culture) is the gold standard; CBNAAT detects rifampicin resistance.**

> Exam pearl: **ATT: 2 months HRZE then HRE, total 9-12 months for osteoarticular TB in India (6-9 months in international guidelines; debated).** **Ethambutol: red-green colour vision; isoniazid: neuropathy (pyridoxine); pyrazinamide: gout and the most hepatotoxic; rifampicin: orange urine and enzyme induction.** **MDR = H plus R resistance.**

> Exam pearl: **Hip TB stage I: flexion, abduction, external rotation with apparent lengthening; stage II onwards: flexion, adduction, internal rotation with apparent then true shortening; stage IV: wandering acetabulum, Girdlestone or arthrodesis.** **Knee triple deformity: flexion, posterior subluxation, external rotation of the tibia.** **Spina ventosa: hand short bones in children; caries sicca: dry shoulder TB; compound palmar ganglion: melon-seed bodies with cross-fluctuation.**
